def: A server that stores images. You push an image to it and servers pull from it. Docker Hub is public; ECR is private to your AWS account.
The label after the colon in an image name, like v1 in quickcart-orders:v1. Tags can be moved to a different image unless the registry forbids it.
One set of file changes in an image, usually made by one Dockerfile line. Layers are shared between images and downloaded only once.
The software that starts and stops containers on a machine, such as Docker or containerd.
The software that splits one physical server into virtual machines, each with its own operating system and kernel.
A software computer with its own operating system and kernel, running on a hypervisor. An EC2 instance is one.
The core of an operating system, which runs programs and talks to the hardware. Every container on a machine shares the host's kernel.
A Linux kernel feature that limits how much CPU and memory a group of processes, such as a container, may use.
The period after a Kubernetes version leaves EKS standard support. The control plane then costs about six times more per hour.
A text file of instructions that Docker runs, top to bottom, to build an image.
A Dockerfile with more than one FROM. Early stages build things; only the last stage becomes the image, so build tools don't ship.
Docker reuses a saved layer when a line and the files it reads haven't changed. Once one line changes, every line below it rebuilds.
A file listing what to leave out of the build context, like .git and .env. It keeps builds fast and secrets out of images.
Storage that Docker creates and manages, mounted into a container. It outlives the container, so a database's files survive docker rm.
A folder on your own machine shown inside a container. Useful for local development; there's no such folder on Fargate.
A Docker network you create with docker network create. Containers on it can reach each other by name, through built-in DNS.
A tool that starts several containers, their network and volumes from one file, compose.yaml. Each service name becomes a hostname.
Connecting a port on the host to a port in a container, like -p 8080:8080. The host's port comes first.
Elastic Container Registry: AWS's private registry for container images, inside your account. ECS and EKS pull images from it.
A repository setting that stops a tag such as v1 ever being moved to a different image, so every version name means exactly one build.
Rules that expire old images from an ECR repository automatically, such as untagged images after 7 days.
ECR image scanning that checks each image for known vulnerabilities as soon as it is pushed. Basic scanning is free.
A sha256 fingerprint calculated from an image's contents. Unlike a tag, it can never point at a different image.
Elastic Container Service: AWS's service for running containers. You describe a task and a desired count, and ECS keeps it running.
A way to run ECS tasks (and EKS pods) with no servers of your own. You pay for the CPU and memory each task asks for.
ECS's recipe for a task: image, CPU, memory, port, logs and roles. Every change makes a new numbered revision.
One running copy of an ECS task definition. On Fargate each task has its own network card and private IP.
Keeps a desired number of ECS tasks running, replaces any that stop, and registers them with a load balancer.
How many tasks an ECS service should run. The service keeps comparing it with what is running and closes the gap.
The IAM role ECS uses before your app starts: pulling the image, sending logs and fetching secrets.
The IAM role your code uses for its own AWS calls while an ECS task runs.
The ECS network mode where each task gets its own network card, private IP and security group. The only mode on Fargate.
The message ECS writes on a stopped task explaining why it stopped. The first place to look when a task won't start.
A release that replaces the old copies of an app with new ones a few at a time, while the service keeps running.
How long a load balancer lets requests already in progress finish on a target it's removing, while sending it nothing new. The default is 300 seconds.
An app hearing the stop signal, finishing the requests it's handling, and then exiting, instead of dying mid-request.
The polite "please stop" signal sent to a container before it's stopped. If the process is still running after the stop timeout, SIGKILL ends it by force.
How long ECS ignores failed load balancer health checks after a task starts, so a slow starter isn't replaced before it's ready.
An ECS setting that stops a release whose new tasks keep failing and, with rollback on, returns the service to the last deployment that worked.
Open-source software that runs containers across many servers and keeps making what's running match the desired state you describe in files.
The smallest thing Kubernetes runs: one or more containers sharing a network address. One running copy of your app, like an ECS task.
A Kubernetes object that says how many pods of which image to run, and replaces them gradually when you release.
Created by a Deployment, one per version: keeps exactly the right number of pods of that version running.
A stable name and address inside a cluster in front of a changing set of ready pods.
A Kubernetes request for a load balancer with routing rules. On EKS, the AWS Load Balancer Controller builds an ALB for it.
A regular check that decides whether a pod gets traffic. A failing pod is taken out of the Service but keeps running.
A regular check that decides whether a container is stuck. When it keeps failing, Kubernetes restarts the container.
A named folder for Kubernetes objects inside one cluster, such as default or kube-system.
Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service: AWS runs the Kubernetes control plane for you; you choose how the nodes run.
The part of Kubernetes that makes decisions: its API, controllers, scheduler and store of desired state. On EKS, AWS runs it for an hourly fee.
A set of EC2 instances that run a cluster's pods. In a managed node group, AWS launches and helps update them.
A program you install in an EKS cluster that builds AWS load balancers when it sees an Ingress, and removes them when the Ingress is deleted.
The command-line tool for talking to a Kubernetes cluster: apply files, list pods, read events, roll releases back.
AWS's command-line tool that creates and deletes a whole EKS cluster, with its nodes and IAM roles, in one command.
What you've declared should be running, such as replicas: 2. Controllers keep comparing reality with it and closing the gap.
